claims.text: The as-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a single-phase FCC matrix.
The as-built alloy has a uniform microstructure and intact grain boundaries.
Elevated-temperature degradation is governed by selective oxidation of Cr and Ti at FCC grain boundaries.
Selective grain-boundary oxidation weakens intergranular cohesion.
Loss of intergranular cohesion can ultimately cause catastrophic failure.
The controlled intervention is exposure to oxidizing versus oxygen-poor atmospheres at elevated temperature.
Above approximately 800°C, diffusion and oxidation kinetics are significant in this alloy.
Exposure for more than approximately 100 hours is sufficient to permit grain-boundary oxidation.
Selective oxidation of Cr and Ti produces continuous oxide films preferentially along grain boundaries.
Continuous grain-boundary oxide films compromise intergranular cohesion and generate microcracks.
Localized grain-boundary oxidation reduces bonding strength between grains and promotes crack initiation and propagation.
Reducing or oxygen-poor conditions minimize oxidation and preserve microstructural integrity relative to oxidizing conditions.
Oxidizing exposure will produce more extensive grain-boundary oxides than reducing or oxygen-poor exposure.
Oxidizing exposure will reduce fracture toughness or tensile strength and may lead to catastrophic failure.
After reducing or oxygen-poor exposure, microstructure and mechanical strength will remain closer to the as-built baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies above 800°C during prolonged exposures for which oxidation kinetics are active.
Outside the stated temperature or duration regime, other degradation mechanisms may dominate.

The mechanism is falsified if oxidizing exposure does not cause greater grain-boundary oxidation and mechanical degradation than the oxygen-poor comparator, or if catastrophic failure does not correlate with intergranular oxides.
